newsitem.title: JAPAN: Taiwan protest intensifies East China Sea isles row.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan protest intensifies East China Sea isles row.

text.p: Egg-throwing protesters briefly took over Japan's quasi-official embassy in Taiwan on Wednesday, intensifying a diplomatic row over ownership of islands in the East China Sea.
Small anti-Japanese demonstrations were also staged in Hong Kong, and plans went ahead for a flotilla to sail from Taiwan to the islands on May 18.
The conservative Japanese parliamentarian who set off the row on Tuesday when he visited the islands said he was considering visiting them again.
Taiwan Foreign Minister John Chang summoned Japan's unofficial envoy Toshio Goto to express Taipei's "indignant concern" over the controversial landing.
The Japanese-administered islands are called Senkaku by Japan, Diaoyu by China and Tiaoyutai by Taiwan, and are claimed by all three.
The dispute over the uninhabited rocky outcrops in the East China Sea threatened to put China and Japan on a new collision course just as ties were returning to normal.
The row has also ignited fiery nationalistic passions in Chinese communities in Hong Kong and Taiwan.
Waters surrounding the islands are rich fishing grounds and are believed to contain unexploited oil and gas reserves.
Japan has claimed the islands, located between Taiwan and Okinawa, since 1895, while China says it has always owned them.
They are located 180 km (115 miles) from Taiwan and about the same distance from islands making up Japan's Okinawa chain.
In Taipei, about 18 activists disguised as visa applicants entered the visa office of Japan's Interchange Association to protest against the landing by the politician and three aides.
The association represents Japanese interests in Taiwan in the absence of diplomatic relations.
Shouting "Down with Japanese militarism", activists pelted counters and walls with eggs, forcing staff to take cover.
"Japan is too coercive and shameless," said Ching Chia-shou, leader of the protesters.
Japanese officials denounced the landing by Shingo Nishimura as an "illegal act" because the owner of the islands did not authorise it, but refused to back down in claiming sovereignty.

"The Japanese government has repeatedly stressed that the islands are territory under Japanese control, but in view of the landowner saying he does not want landings or other activities on the islands, it was an illegal act," Japan's top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference.
"The landing was also not a good idea from the point of view of foreign relations," Kajiyama added.
The decades-old dispute was rekindled last year when a right-wing group from Japan built a makeshift lighthouse on the islands.
A Hong Kong activist who joined a protest flotilla last September drowned when he jumped into stormy waters to press China's claim.

The latest episode has been an embarrassment for Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who hopes to exchange visits with his Chinese counterpart Li Peng later this year to mark the 25th anniversary of bilateral ties.
In recent months, Beijing-Tokyo ties, including a resumption of Japanese aid, have got back on track after they were frozen over China's nuclear testing.
Nishimura's political party, the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), distanced itself from the landing, saying it was a private act in which the party had no involvement.
Nishimura, until Tuesday's landing an obscure junior legislator whose Osaka constituency is at least 1,000 km (600 miles) from the disputed islands, was unbowed by the criticism.
"I have no regrets. It was something I had to do," he told a news conference. "The Japanese government has stooped so low that it has developed a kow-tow policy towards China."
Nishimura said he might visit the islands again, even on May 18, to coincide with the planned visit by the boats from Taiwan.
"We are planning a large-scale action on May 18, taking boats to near the Diaoyus and (will) swim ashore. We plan to land on the island and stay there overnight," Ching said.
Ching said his committee would join forces with activists from Hong Kong to declare "our sovereignty over the Diaoyu islands".
